paragraphs.heading: 20.3 Disorders of Phosphate Homeostasis – 504

paragraphs.text: Extracellular phosphate is a critical compo nent of the skeleton that plays an important role in modulating skeletal processes like growth plate maturation and skeletal mineral ization. Phosphate homeostasis is regulated by dietary intake and the mineral ionregulating hormones parathyroid hormone (PTH) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF23). Furthermore, disorders disrupting phosphate homeostasis have resulted in a greater under standing of the molecular regulation of phos phate balance as well as the hormones that modulate these processes.
paragraphs.heading: 20.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Extracellular phosphate is a critical compo nent of the skeleton that, in combination with calcium, is essential for mineralization of newly formed osteoid. Growing children have positive phosphate balance to support skeletal growth, while healthy adults have a zero phos phate balance. Phosphate deficiency leads to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Phosphate accounts for about 0.6% of the body weight at birth and about 1% of body weight in the adult [1]. Eighty-five percent of phosphate is in the skeleton and in teeth, while 15% of phosphate is located in soft tissue and extracellular fluid [2].
paragraphs.heading: 20.2 Phosphate Homeostasis

paragraphs.text: In plasma, phosphate exists in either inor ganic or organic forms; the latter primarily as phospholipids and phosphate esters [3]. The total plasma concentration of phosphate in an adult is about 14 mg/dL, of which 4 mg/dL is inorganic phosphate (Pi). Ten to fifteen per cent of inorganic phosphate (Pi) is protein bound and the remainder is filtered at the renal glomeruli and is usually complexed with sodium, calcium, or magnesium.
paragraphs.heading: 20.2 Phosphate Homeostasis

paragraphs.text: About 70% of phosphate filtered by the glomeruli is reabsorbed in the proximal con voluted tubule, while 10% of phosphate is reabsorbed in the proximal straight tubule, and <10% in the distal segments of the neph ron. Thus, the proximal tubule of the kidney is where a majority of the phosphate reab
paragraphs.heading: 20.2 Phosphate Homeostasis

paragraphs.text: sorbed from the filtered load [4]. Renal reab sorption of phosphate progressively increases as more is filtered, until a maximum tubular reabsorption rate for phosphate (TmP) is reached, after which phosphate excretion increases in proportion with the filtered load. TmP can vary even within the same person due in part to differences in GFR, therefore TmP is normalized to GFR (TmP/GFR, max imum tubular reabsorption of phosphate per unit volume of GFR), when quantifying renal tubular phosphate reabsorption [2]. In renal tubular cells, filtered phosphate is reclaimed by sodium (Na+)-dependent phosphate (Pi) transporters at the apical brush border mem brane. Phosphate is then translocated across the cell and returned to the blood circulation at the basolateral membrane, a process that is mediated by the Na+/K+-dependent ATPase [5] and possibly the xenotropic and polytropic retroviral receptor 1 (XPR1) [6].

Type II Na/Pi co-transporters include three highly homologous isoforms, including Type IIa (NPT2a, SLC34A1), Type IIc (NPT2c, SLC24A3), and Type IIb (NPT2b, SLC34A2). NPT2a and NPT2c, expressed on the brush border membrane of renal proxi mal tubules, are the predominant regulators of phosphate reabsorption in renal tubules. In mice, protein levels of NPT2a are approxi mately tenfold higher than those of NPT2c [3]. In contrast, NPT2b is not expressed in the kidney, but it is instead expressed in several other tissues, including lung and particularly the small intestine [7–10]. The ubiquitously expressed type III Na/Pi co-transporters are retroviral cell surface receptors (gibbon ape leukemia virus (Glvr-1, PiT-1, SLC20A1) and murine amphotropic virus (Ram-1, Pit-2, SLC20A2) that are [11, 12] localized to all segments of the nephron at the basolateral membrane and mediate cellular phosphate balance.

Sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter type IIb (NPT2b, SLC34A2) plays an important role in sodium-phosphatedependent phosphate resorption in the small intestine. Type III sodium-dependent phos phate co-transporters PiT1 and PiT2 contrib ute to phosphate resorption in the small

intestine, but less so than NPT2b [13]. Mutations in PiT2 have been associated with development of brain calcifications in humans and mice. Thus, affected individuals develop familial basal ganglia calcifications (Fahr’s Disease) and mice lacking PiT2 have elevated phosphate levels in their cerebral spinal fluid [14, 15]. About 60–65% of dietary intake of phosphate is absorbed by the small intestine, where in response to an increasing dietary load [1]. If an adult is in zero phosphate bal ance, the intestinal absorption of phosphate is equal to the amount of phosphate excreted by the kidney. In growing children, the net amount of phosphate excreted is less than the amount absorbed by the small intestine, thus resulting in positive phosphate balance [16]. Because serum phosphate concentrations vary throughout the day depending on dietary phosphate intake and oral phosphate supple mentation, collection of a fasting blood sam ple is preferred for clinical analysis.
FGF23, a “phosphatonin,” is a secreted FGF and critical regulator of phosphate homeosta sis. It is predominantly expressed in bone, spe
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.2 FGF23

paragraphs.text: cifically osteocytes and at lower levels in osteoblasts [24, 25]. In the presence of the cofactor Klotho, FGF23 binds to FGFR1 with high affinity [26]. FGFR1 is the predominant receptor for FGF23 action, with FGFR4 likely playing a minor role in the phosphaturic effect when activated by FGF23 [27, 28]. FGF23 decreases serum phosphate levels by reducing expression of NPT2a and NPT2c in the renal tubule cells and decreasing the pro duction of 1,25(OH)2D. As documented in mice, FGF23 regulates 1,25(OH)2D levels by down-regulating expression of Cyp27b1, which encodes 1α-hydroxylase, and it upregu lates Cyp24a1, which encodes an enzyme that catabolizes 1,25(OH)2D, thus decreasing cir culating levels of 1,25(OH)2D. Tmem174, a transmembrane protein localized in the renal proximal tubules, interacts with Npt2a, but not Npt2c to prevent hyperphosphatemia, thus contributing to the regulation of FGF23 levels [29, 30].
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.2 FGF23

paragraphs.text: Genetic linkage studies identified the genetic cause of autosomal dominant hypo phosphatemic rickets (ADHR), which is caused by FGF23 mutations affecting either Arg176 or Arg179 that render the intact, biologically active hormone resistant to inac tivation by cleavage [31]. In the presence of these mutations, iron deficiency increases intact FGF23 levels [32, 33]. Furthermore, some small, usually benign tumors excrete abundant amounts of FGF23 thereby induc ing urinary phosphate-wasting and osteoma lacia (TIO) [24] that is most likely triggered by expression of a chimeric FGFR/fibronectin protein [34]. Affected patients present with low serum levels of phosphate and 1,25(OH)2D resulting in clinical symptoms that are similar to those observed in other hypophosphatemic disorders.
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.2 FGF23

paragraphs.text: like proprotein convertase [36] ( Fig. 20.2). Homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in DMP1 [38], FAM20C [39], and ENPP1 [40], as well as het erozygous or hemizygous PHEX mutations [41] lead to elevated circulating levels of FGF23 in mice and humans, and thus hypo phosphatemia. FAM20C regulates the phos phorylation of Ser180 in FGF23 which blocks O-glycosylation at Thr178, and thus enhances FGF23 cleavage [37].
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.2 FGF23

paragraphs.text: Glycerol-3-phosphate (G-3-P), a down stream product of glycolysis, is converted in the kidney, but also in other tissues, into lyso phosphatidic acid (LPA), which stimulates FGF23 production. It is conceivable that
G-3-P serves as a sensor for phosphate levels in the kidney, where phosphate stimulates kidney-specific glycolysis, and thus G-3-P and subsequently production [42].

Parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulates serum phosphate levels by increasing internalization and subsequent lysosomal degradation of NPT2a, thus promoting urinary phosphate excretion [43, 44]. On the basolateral mem brane of the proximal renal tubules, PTH binds to PTH/PTHrP receptors (PTHR1), which activates at least two second messenger systems, namely cAMP leading to the activa tion of protein kinase A (PKA) and intracel
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.3 PTH

paragraphs.text: lular calcium and IP3 leading to the activation of protein kinase C (PKC). Both pathways then activate ERK/MAPK signaling to induce internalization of NPT2a [45, 46]. Furthermore, the PTHR1 can interact with NHERF2 at the renal apical brush border membrane, thereby stabilizing NPT2a protein on the cell surface and preventing desensitiza tion of the PTH signal [47]. Humans with het erozygous NHERF1 mutations may present with hypophosphatemia and renal phosphatewasting [48, 49].
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.3 PTH

paragraphs.text: Dietary phosphate and serum phosphate lev els are important regulators of 1,25(OH)2D. Dietary restriction in rats or mice leads to hypophosphatemia, which enhances vitamin D 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) mRNA expression and protein levels in the renal proximal tubule by six- to eightfold [50], thereby increasing the produc tion of 1,25(OH)2D [51]. Furthermore, dietary phosphate restriction in mice decreases renal 24-hydroxylase activity and expression, thus
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.4 Vitamin D

paragraphs.text: resulting in decreased catabolism of 1,25(OH)2D [52, 53]. On the other hand, treat ment of vitamin D-deficient rats with 1,25(OH)2D enhances NPT2a mRNA expres sion and protein in the renal brush border membrane [54]. Consistent with the findings in animal studies, dietary phosphate restric tion in humans increases serum 1,25(OH)2D levels, while phosphate supplementation has the opposite effect [55].
paragraphs.heading: 20.2.1.4 Vitamin D

paragraphs.text: Chronic hypophosphatemia is usually asymp tomatic, though affected individuals can com plain of myalgias. In mice, deletion of both PiT1 and PiT2 in skeletal muscle resulted in hypophosphatemia and muscle atrophy, dem onstrating that these phosphate transporters are required for skeletal myofiber function and survival [56]. Moderate to severe hypo

Rhabdomyolysis associated with low serum phosphate is most commonly a consequence of chronic alcoholism [58, 59]. A combination of factors, including inappropriate phospha turia, gastrointestinal loss, hyperventilation, or infusion of dextrose-containing fluids, can contribute to hypophosphatemia in alcohol ism [57].

paragraphs.heading: of Hypophosphatemia and Hyperphosphatemia

paragraphs.text: Hematologic consequences of hypophos phatemia may include hemolysis or leukocyte dysfunction. Adequate phosphate levels are necessary to maintain ATP levels in red blood cells and leukocytes [60]. Consequently, a fall in ATP levels from hypophosphatemia has been associated with decreased red blood life span, cases of hemolytic anemia [61–63], and impaired leukocyte cell function [64, 65].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3 Disorders of Phosphate

paragraphs.text: Hypophosphatemia can result in respira tory muscle weakness, including impaired contraction of the diaphragm, leading to impaired respiratory function [66, 67]. In hos pitalized patients who had low phosphate lev els, improvement in respiratory muscle function was observed with phosphate reple tion. Severe, acute, or chronic hypophospha temia can compromise myocardial function [68, 69]. However, a study of pediatric patients with chronic hypophosphatemia from X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) demon strated no alteration in left ventricular func tion [70]. Central and peripheral nervous system dysfunction has been reported in patients with acute severe hypophosphatemia after developing re-feeding syndrome [71, 72]. Patients may manifest with irritability and muscle weakness and progress to confusion or coma [72, 73].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3 Disorders of Phosphate

paragraphs.text: A high serum phosphate level is usually not associated with significant symptoms, but can lead to the formation of ectopic calcifica tions by precipitating in the soft tissues as calcium-phosphate deposits. Such calcifica tions are observed in chronic renal failure, hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathy roidism, or tumoral calcinosis, all of which are typically characterized by elevated serum phosphate levels. Biochemical consequences
paragraphs.heading: 20.3 Disorders of Phosphate

paragraphs.text: Fanconi’s syndrome is characterized by impaired proximal renal tubule function due to genetic or secondary causes, leading to proximal renal tubular acidosis, and renal losses of amino acids, glucose, bicarbonate, potassium, and phosphate. The hypophos phatemia can result in osteomalacia and rick ets, with bowing of the legs and short stature [74]. Therefore, phosphate supplementation and/or calcitriol treatment are used to treat the consequences of low serum phosphate lev els. Multiple disorders are complicated by Fanconi’s syndrome. For instance, majority of cases have an acquired form of Fanconi’s syn drome due to secondary causes that may include burn injuries, exposure to certain medications or toxic metals, or a variety of other conditions like multiple myeloma, or amyloidosis [74]. Furthermore, rare inherited disorders like cystinosis, Wilson’s disease, Lowe syndrome, type I glycogen storage dis ease, or galactosemia can lead to renal phos phate wasting. Medications like tenofovir, an anti-retroviral medication used for treatment of HIV/AIDS, is well-documented to be asso ciated with Fanconi’s syndrome-related hypo phosphatemia [75]. Patients infected with acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) who have severe disease requiring hospitalization may have a higher incidence of hypophosphatemia associated with acute kidney injury. It is hypothesized that SARS-CoV-2 infection involving the proximal renal tubules may lead to Fanconi’s syndrome [76].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.1 Fanconi’s Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Furthermore, Fanconi’s syndrome has also been described in families with fully pen etrant heterozygous missense autosomal dominant mutations in glycine amidinotrans ferase (GATM), an enzyme prominently expressed in the renal proximal tubules that regulates creatine synthesis. Affected patients develop Fanconi’s syndrome with hyperphos phaturia but no rickets or bone deformities as children, and they may progress to renal fibro sis and end-stage kidney failure as adults [77, 78].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.1 Fanconi’s Syndrome

paragraphs.text: The type II sodium phosphate co-transporter (NPT2a, SLC23A1) is expressed exclusively in the brush border membrane of renal proximal tubular cells. Deletion of Npt2a in mice results in enhanced renal phosphate-wasting, leading to hypophosphatemia, a decrease in serum FGF23 levels, and a compensatory increase in serum 1,25(OH)2D levels. The increase in 1,25(OH)2D increases intestinal calcium absorption and results in hypercalce mia, hypercalciuria, and suppressed PTH lev els [79, 80]. The age-dependent increase in serum 1,25(OH)2D levels correlated with the improvement of rickets in these mice, suggest ing that the enhanced 1,25(OH)2D action can compensate for hypophosphatemia in regulat ing growth plate maturation and growth [79].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.1.1 NPT2a Mutations

paragraphs.text: An autosomal recessive form of renal Fanconi’s syndrome was described in 1988 in two siblings, who had marked hypophospha temia, and elevated 1,25(OH)2D levels, as well as rickets, growth retardation, and skeletal deformities [81]. Both siblings were later shown to have homozygous loss-of-function mutations in SLC34A1 (encodes NPT2a) and that their biochemical abnormalities greatly improved, although renal function remained abnormal [82]. Recently, numerous other homozygous or compound heterozygous NPT2a mutations were described in several infants, who presented with severe hypercalce mia and renal phosphate-wasting, and sup pressed serum PTH levels. Approximately half of the infants in this cohort had elevated serum 1,25(OH)2D levels associated with
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.1.1 NPT2a Mutations

paragraphs.text: hypercalcemia. These metabolic abnormali ties resolved with phosphate supplementation [83], thus potentially preventing nephrocalci nosis. Mice lacking Npt2a fed high phosphate diets with or without high calcium were more likely to develop renal calcifications compared to wild-type mice fed a similar diet, suggesting that optimization of dietary content of phos phate and calcium are needed for proper treat ment of affected individuals [84].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.1.1 NPT2a Mutations

paragraphs.text: Furthermore, two heterozygous mutations were identified in the SLC34A1 gene (A48P and V147M). The affected individuals pre sented with idiopathic hypophosphatemia, recurrent kidney stones, and osteomalacia [85]. Other heterozygous SLC34A1 mutations (91del7, A133V, H568Y) have been reported in a cohort of patients who have recurrent kidney stones but no hypercalciuria, hypo phosphatemia, or increased urinary phos phate excretion [86].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.1.1 NPT2a Mutations

paragraphs.text: Patients with documented SLC34A3 mutations have a significantly increased likeli hood of developing kidney stones. Forty-six percent of subjects with SLC34A3 mutations on both alleles manifest nephrocalcinosis compared with 6% of non-affected family members [92]. Even heterozygous carriers of SLC34A3 mutations have a higher frequency of renal calcifications that are intermediate to those with homozygous/compound heterozy gous mutations and subjects without such mutations. The likelihood of renal calcifica tions increased with the severity of hypophos phatemia and decreased tubular reabsorption of phosphate [92].

paragraphs.text: XLH is the most frequent inherited form of hypophosphatemia, with a reported incidence of 1:20,000 [93]. It is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern with complete penetrance, thought there is wide phenotypic variation, even within the same family. Establishing the diagnosis of XLH can be delayed until adult hood due to lack of awareness of phosphate levels or expression of a mild phenotype. When a more severe phenotype is present, children typically manifest rickets by age 1–2 years, causing growth retardation and bowed legs. On radiographs, the growth plates of long bones appear abnormal, with expan sion and fraying of the metaphyses [94]. There is discordant growth between the lower extremity long bones and the torso, with the growth retardation being more apparent in the long bones of the legs [95]. Children with XLH can manifest premature cranial synosto sis and often develop dental abscesses and caries due to defective dentoalveolar mineral ization [96, 97]. Adults may manifest with pseudofractures, osteoarthritis, osteophytes, or enthesopathy, which is the abnormal min eralization of the bone-tendon attachment sites, such as the Achilles or patellar entheses
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemia (XLH)

paragraphs.text: [98, 99]. Hypophosphatemia is often associ ated with myalgias, though many XLH patients are often asymptomatic from the hypophosphatemia [2]. As adults, XLH patients also report tinnitus and conductive hearing loss. Similarly, mice with XLH have conductive hearing loss, which is associated with hypomineralization of the auditory ossi cles [100].
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemia (XLH)

paragraphs.text: 20.1 Hyp mice are a murine equivalent of human XLH. These mice carry a deletion in the 3′ region of the Phex gene [103]. The Hyp mouse mimics the XLH phenotype seen in humans, including biochemical abnormali ties, growth retardation, rickets/osteomalacia, and enthesopathy.
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemia (XLH)

paragraphs.text: XLH is caused by inactivating mutations in the PHEX gene, which is located on chromo some Xp22.1 [104]. Over 800 mutations have been reported in PHEX [105], including mis sense, frameshift, nonsense, duplication, and insertion mutations [106, 107]. PHEX muta tions are catalogued on the website www. db.mcgill.ca. PHEX is predominantly expressed in bone, specifically in osteocytes and osteoblasts. It is also expressed in other tissues such as lung, brain, and teeth, but at lower levels [41, 108]. Although it is known that serum FGF23 levels are elevated in patients with PHEX mutations, the underly ing regulatory mechanisms contributing these FGF23 elevation are not known; PHEX does not directly contribute to cleaving and thus inactivating FGF23 [109, 110]. Although studies demonstrated that PHEX binds to
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: and cleaves the triphosphorylated acidic, ser ine-, and aspartic acid-rich motif (ASARM) in proteins like MEPE to block their inhibi tion of mineralization [111], the physiological target(s) of the PHEX endopeptidase cur rently remains to be defined.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Analysis of genetically modified mice have supported the pathogenic roles of PHEX and FGF23 in causing hypophosphatemia and rickets in XLH. Conditional ablation of PHEX in osteoblasts (using the osteocalcin promoter) leads to elevated serum FGF23 lev els, low serum phosphate levels, and decreased renal Npt2a expression, resulting in poor skel etal mineralization [41]. Conversely, trans genic overexpression of PHEX under the control of the pro-alpha1(I) collagen pro moter improved the skeletal mineralization in Hyp mice, but it did not normalize serum phosphate levels [112]. Furthermore, overex pression of FGF23 under the alpha1(I) colla gen promoter resulted in impaired growth and hypophosphatemic rickets due to phosphatu ria secondary to decreased renal expression of Npt2a [113]. Deletion of FGF23 from Hyp mice improved serum phosphate and 1,25(OH)2D levels, but did not normalize skeletal mineralization or growth, indicating that PHEX-specific actions aside from its abil ity to regulate FGF23 likely modulate these processes [25]. Overexpression of FGF23 in rat calvarial osteoblasts decreased mineraliza tion and nodule formation, while bone forma tion in parietal organ cultures was decreased [114]. Treatment of wild-type calvarial osteo blasts with recombinant FGF23 furthermore suppressed formation of mineralized nodules in vitro [115]. These studies indicate that FGF23 may suppress mineralization indepen dent of its effect on phosphate homeostasis. Thus, abnormal skeletal mineralization result ing in the XLH phenotype is not only due to abnormal mineral ion and hormone homeo stasis, but likely involves additional molecular defects that are incompletely characterized. It has been reported that the mineralization inhibitor osteopontin is elevated in Hyp bone and that deletion of this PHEX target mod estly improved skeletal mineralization in these
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: mice [116]. Also, osteocytes in Hyp mice show decreased expression of tissue nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, which regulates miner alization by metabolizing pyrophosphate (PPi), a potent mineralization inhibitor. These findings suggest that abnormal PPi homeosta sis in XLH bones could contribute to the development of osteomalacia [117]. Furthermore, implantation of Hyp osteo blasts into wild-type mice did not normalize the osteoid volume of the transplants, thus indicating an intrinsic osteoblast defect in XLH [118]. When wild-type osteoblasts were grown in medium with phosphate concentra tions similar to those of serum levels in wildtype mice, alkaline phosphatase activity increased. In contrast, Hyp osteoblasts failed to respond to 1,25(OH)2D treatment when exposed to the same phosphate concentration, thus demonstrating that Hyp osteoblasts have an abnormal response to 1,25(OH)2D [119].

Extracellular phosphate is essential for normal growth plate maturation [120–122]. Mice lacking the vitamin D receptor and Hyp mice fed normal chow as well as mice fed a low phosphate diet all have hypophosphate mia and an expansion of growth plates (hyper trophic layer). Hypophosphatemia impairs Erk1/2 activation, which in turn results in an expansion of the hypertrophic chondrocyte layer demonstrating the critical role of phos phate in regulating growth plate maturation [120, 122]. PTHrP action appears to contrib ute to the growth plate expansion observed during hypophosphatemia because mice het erozygous for PTHLH ablation (the gene encoding PTHrP) did not develop the antici pated growth plate changes when fed a low phosphate diet [123]. Mice and humans with XLH often have elevated serum PTH levels and Hyp mice have increased expression of PTHrP at the peri-articular surface. Consequently, actions of PTH or PTHrP are likely to contribute to the impaired growth plate maturation seen in XLH.
1,25(OH)2D is also an important regulator of growth and skeletal mineralization and structure in XLH, aside from its ability to modulate serum calcium and phosphate lev

els. Hyp mice that are null for the vitamin D 24-hydroxylase (Cyp24a1) or that transgeni cally express FGF23 revealed significantly improved rickets/osteomalacia despite persis tent hypophosphatemia [124]. Although serum 1,25(OH)2D levels decreased paradoxi cally in these mice, there was an increase in local tissue production of 1,25(OH)2D [124]. In addition, treatment of Hyp mice with calcitriol alone restored Npt2a expres sion in the kidney, significantly improved growth and growth plate maturation, as well as skeletal microarchitecture/biomechanics and dentoalveolar mineralization. Treatment of Hyp mice with calcitriol alone was superior to anti-FGF23 antibody therapy despite increased serum levels of FGF23 observed with 1,25D treatment and both treatments increasing serum phosphate to similar levels [93, 125].

Treatment of Hyp mice with either calcitriol alone or with the anti-FGF23 antibody blocks BMP/IHH sig naling in the entheses and prevents enthesopa thy in the Hyp mice, also pointing to a role for impaired 1,25(OH)2D action in regulating the abnormal mineralization of the entheses observed in XLH [129] ( Fig. 20.4). Taken together, these studies support an important role for 1,25(OH)2D in the pathogenesis of the different skeletal aspects of XLH.

Treatment for XLH in children is predomi nantly aimed at improving their growth, to minimize rickets/osteomalacia, and thus to prevent bowing and orthopedic procedures. Traditionally, children with XLH were treated with a combination of oral phosphate, given multiple times per day, and calcitriol, from the time of diagnosis until active growth has stopped. Treatment with phosphate and cal citriol therapy decreases alkaline phosphatase levels and improves, but does not normalize, skeletal growth and mineralization [94, 101]. Serum phosphate levels do not normalize because of persistent renal phosphate losses due to elevated circulating FGF23 levels, which can increase even further above base line during treatment [130].
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Complications of conventional therapy may include hypercalciuria or hypercalcemia from calcitriol therapy [131]. Also, the doses of phosphate (and compliance with this medi cation) and calcitriol are thought to be correlated with the development of nephro calcinosis, which can lead to compromised renal function [132]. Phosphate therapy alone should be avoided because it leads to second ary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, requir ing parathyroid surgery [133]. Treatment of
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: mice with XLH with calcitriol starting on day 2 (prior to enthesis changes) can prevent the development of enthesopathy [129], but treat ing Hyp mice with calcitriol and phosphate starting at day 30 (after enthesis maturation) did not prevent or reduce the extent of enthe sopathies [134], suggesting early and consis tent therapy is needed to attenuate the development of mineralization at the tendonbone insertion sites.

Due to the lack of normalization of the XLH phenotype with conventional therapy, an antibody targeting FGF23, burosumab (Crysvita), was developed. It was FDAapproved for the treatment of children and adults with XLH. Given the efficacy of buro sumab in improving serum biochemistries, skeletal mineralization, and potentially growth, it has largely replaced conventional therapy as the treatment of choice for XLH. However, treated children continued to develop dental abscesses, and the effects of burosumab on the development of enthesopa thies or osteoarthritis has not yet been reported. Studies in Hyp mice comparing an anti-FGF23 blocking antibody (from Amgen) with daily calcitriol therapy (without phos phate supplementation) revealed that daily calcitriol was superior to the antibody in improving growth plate morphology, long bone growth, bone histomorphometric parameters, as well as skeletal mineralization and biomechanics [93]. Thus, calcitriol alone or in combination with burosumab may potentially be alternative treatment options for XLH patients. For further details on XLH treatment, please refer to Chap. 21.

Interestingly, some of the ADHR patients who present with the disorder during child hood had normalization of phosphate levels after puberty [135, 136] and one patient pre sented with severe hypophosphatemia and osteomalacia only after several uncompli cated pregnancies [137].
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ADHR)

paragraphs.text: Econs and McEnery described a large kin dred, in which affected individuals presented with hypophosphatemia and/or rickets at variable ages, ranging from early childhood to adolescence and adulthood; the mode of inheritance was autosomal dominant [135, 138]. After linking the genetic locus of ADHR to chromosome 12p13, Econs and colleagues identified heterozygous missense FGF23 mutations in several different families (R176Q, R179Q, and R179W) [31]. These FGF23 mutations in ADHR patients render FGF23 resistant to cleavage, thus increasing the amount of intact biologically active FGF23 in the circulation [35, 136, 139–141].
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ADHR)

paragraphs.text: ADHR can become apparent with onset of iron deficiency, such as with the start of menses during puberty or during the postpar tum period. In patients with ADHR, serum iron levels are inversely correlated with intact and C-terminal FGF23 levels. Consequently, the lower the iron levels the higher the levels of biologically active FGF23, which reduce serum phosphate levels. In unaffected con trols, only the C-terminal FGF23 levels cor relate with iron levels while intact levels do not [33]. Iron supplementation of iron-deficient adults with ADHR normalized serum FGF23 levels and increased serum phosphate levels [142]. Consistent with the human ADHR phe notype, mice engineered to express FGF23 with the R176Q mutation that are fed an irondeficient diet developed elevated FGF23 levels [32]. These studies emphasize the important role of iron in maintaining normal phosphate homeostasis. They also highlight the impor tance of determining the ratio of intact FGF23 to C-terminal fragments for assessing the regulation of phosphate balance.
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ADHR)

paragraphs.text: 144 Loss-of-function mutations of the ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/pyrophosphodi esterase 1 (ENPP1) gene have been implicated in ARHR [145]. ENPP1 hydrolyzing ATP into pyrophosphate (PPi), an inhibitor of mineral ization, thereby regulating skeletal mineraliza tion [146]. Therefore, patients and mice with loss-of-function mutations in ENPP1 develop ectopic calcifications of the aorta, kidney, and spine. Patients with ENPP1 mutations may present in infancy with generalized arterial cal cification of infancy, with variable calcification of medium and large vessel arteries that can be life-threatening. Like patients with ENPP1 mutations, mice lacking ENPP1 have hypo phosphatemia, undetectable PPi levels, and elevated FGF23 serum levels [147, 148]. Thus, in addition to its role in modulating skeletal mineralization, ENPP1 also regulates phos phate homeostasis and FGF23. As with XLH, patients with ARHR can manifest early onset
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ARHR)

paragraphs.text: hearing loss, mineralizing enthesopathies, and ossification of the posterior longitudinal liga ment of the spine [40, 145, 149]. During ado lescence, serum FGF23 levels begin to rise, leading to hypophosphatemia and rickets; the severity of the rachitic phenotype is variable and correlates with serum FGF23 levels [150, 151]. Limited case reports show that conven tional therapy with phosphate and calcitriol supplementation does not worsen arterial cal cifications [150]. However, the use of the anti- FGF23 antibody burosumab in an affected patient resulted in worsening cardiac and vas cular calcifications [152]. More recently, ENPP1-null mice treated with humanized ENPP1-Fc prevented organ and cardiovascu lar calcifications, increased pyrophosphate lev els, and improved growth and skeletal microarchitecture, pointing to a potential ben eficial role for ENPP1 enzyme replacement therapy in treating affected patients [153].
paragraphs.heading: Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ARHR)

paragraphs.text: In Fibrous Dysplasia (FD), normal bone is replaced by fibrous tissue. It can affect one bone (monoostotic) or multiple bones (poly ostotic) in the craniofacial, appendicular, or axial skeleton [157]. Children with this disor der usually present by 10 years of age with bone pain, fracture, or progressive deformity.
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.2.4 Fibrous Dysplasia (FD)

paragraphs.text: FD can manifest on its own or be part of McCune–Albright syndrome, which is caused by somatic post-zygotic mutations in GNAS, the gene encoding Gsα, which mediates the actions of numerous G protein-coupled recep tors that use the cAMP/PKA signaling path way [158]; these missense mutations responsible for McCune–Albright syndrome affect only one of two amino acid residues, Arg201 or Gln227 [159]. Affected patients typically have café-au-lait spots and endocri nopathies reflecting abnormal signaling by GPCRs, which can include gonadotropinindependent precocious puberty, thyroid lesions with or without hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, hypercortisolism, or testicular lesions with Leydig and/or Sertoli cell hyperplasia [160].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.2.4 Fibrous Dysplasia (FD)

paragraphs.text: FD patients may have hypophosphatemia and corresponding low or inappropriately normal serum 1,25(OH)2D levels due to ele vated serum FGF23 levels [161]. The degree of urine phosphate-wasting and disease bur den correlates with FGF23 serum levels [162]. Although fibrous lesions in FD express FGF23, overt hypophosphatemia and classic hypophosphatemic rickets are not frequently observed. It has been shown that there is altered FGF23 cleavage due to decreased gly cosylation and increased furin activity in bone marrow stromal cells isolated from FD sub jects, thus possibly explaining the lack of a rachitic phenotype in FD [163]. These studies suggest Gsα plays a role in the regulation of FGF23 metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.2.4 Fibrous Dysplasia (FD)

paragraphs.text: The bone pain associated with FD may be more severe in adults than in children, and can be treated with bisphosphonates. Treatment with bisphosphonates has also been shown to decrease serum FGF23 levels and increase in serum 1,25(OH)2D levels [161]. However, there may be an increased risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw in FD patients on bisphosphonate therapy [164]. There is lim ited data on the efficacy of denosumab (anti- RANKL antibody) in therapy for FD. Administration of denosumab to fibrous dysplasia patients can decrease bone turnover markers, bone pain, and expansion of bony lesions. Thus, its use should be closely moni tored in patients, as treatment with deno
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.2.4 Fibrous Dysplasia (FD)

paragraphs.text: sumab has been reported to cause worsening hypophosphatemia and secondary hyperpara thyroidism [165]. Discontinuation of deno sumab treatment can be complicated by rebound osteoclast activation, leading to hypercalcemia [166]. However, a pediatric patient with McCune–Albright Syndrome/ Fibrous dysplasia with frank hypophosphate mia and rickets was treated with burosumab, leading to improvement in mineral ion homeo stasis, decreased fractures, and improved bone pain and strength [167].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.2.4 Fibrous Dysplasia (FD)

paragraphs.text: Linear nevus sebaceous syndrome (LNSS), also known as epidermal nevus syndrome (ENS) is a rare, sporadic, and highly variable disorder that is characterized by papilloma tous epidermal hyperplasia and abnormalities in multiple organ systems, including neuro logic, ophthalmic, cardiovascular, and uro genital deformities [168]. LNSS/ENS is associated with elevated serum FGF23 levels and overtly low serum levels of 1,25(OH)2D, leading to hypophosphatemic rickets; the source of the FGF23 had not yet been identi fied [169, 170]. Whole exome sequencing iden tified somatic post-zygotic activating mutations of the HRAS or NRAS genes in affected skin and bone tissue from ENS patients with elevated serum FGF23 levels, suggesting that RAS signaling may play a role in regulating FGF23 [170]. These skin lesions do not express FGF23 mRNA or protein. In affected patients, extensive removal of these lesions failed to improve the hypophosphate mia [171]. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the excess FGF23 could be synthesized by dysplastic bone lesions.
paragraphs.heading: Syndrome (LNSS)/Epidermal Nevus Syndrome (ENS)

paragraphs.text: 34 TIO patients have rickets/osteomalacia and an increased incidence of fractures. Tumors found in patients with TIO are pre dominantly of mesenchymal in origin and are often very slow growing and are located in obscure or inaccessible areas such as the naso pharynx or mandible, making them difficult to localize and causing significant delays in diagnosis from few months to 19 years [179]. Since somatostatin receptors are often highly expressed on phosphaturic tumors, imaging modalities using radioisotopes to target these receptors are effective in localizing tumors. The 68Ga-DOTATE PET/CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting tumors [180, 181]. Also, 18FDG-PET/CT aids in the detection of lesions of high metabolic activity. Surgical resection is curative for TIO, but if the tumor cannot be found or completely resected, therapy with calcitriol and phos phate supplementation or burosumab can help improve the metabolic and bone abnor malities [179, 182].

20.5 While tumoral calcinosis is predominantly sporadic, but it can be inherited as an autoso mal recessive disorder. The genetic defects underlying tumoral calcinosis include muta tions in the genes encoding FGF23, GALNT3, or Klotho, all of which lead to impaired FGF23 action. Full-length FGF23 is either destabilized, not secreted due to retention in the Golgi apparatus, or there is resistance to intact, biologically active FGF23 [195, 196]. In these cases, affected individuals had increased circulating levels of the biologically inactive C-terminal FGF23 fragments and decreased circulating levels of intact FGF23 [195, 196].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.3.1 Tumoral Calcinosis

paragraphs.text: UDP-N-acetyl-alpha-d-galactosam ine:polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 3 (GALNT3) mediates the mucin-type O-glycosylation of FGF23 at a subtilisin-like pro-protein convertase recogni tion sequence motif, which is essential for the secretion of biologically active intact FGF23 [197]. Homozygous or compound heterozy gous GALNT3 mutations have been reported to result in defects in the post-translational modification of FGF23 [198, 199]. Circulating levels of intact FGF23 are normal or low, while C-terminal fragments of FGF23 are elevated [198, 200]. Compound heterozygous GALNT3 mutations have also been reported
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.3.1 Tumoral Calcinosis

paragraphs.text: in patients who presented with hyperostosis of the tibia combined with hyperphosphatemia and elevated 1,25(OH)2D levels, suggesting hyperostosis-hyperphosphatemia syndrome may be a continuum of the tumoral calcinosis phenotype. Like other cases of tumoral calci nosis, this patient also had elevated circulating levels of C-terminal FGF23 fragments and low levels of intact FGF23 [201].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.3.1 Tumoral Calcinosis

paragraphs.text: A homozygous mutation in Klotho, which encodes the co-receptor for FGF23, has been reported in a patient who presented with severe vascular and soft tissue calcifications, as well as increased serum levels of phosphate, cal cium, PTH, and 1,25(OH)2D [202]. Both mice and humans with homozygous Klotho muta tions have elevated circulating levels of intact FGF23 and develop ectopic soft tissue and vascular calcifications. The His193Arg muta tion in Klotho destabilizes the Klotho protein, thereby decreasing its production and secre tion [202]. In the absence of Klotho, FGF23 was unable to bind to FGFR1, its receptor.
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.3.1 Tumoral Calcinosis

paragraphs.text: Although low serum phosphate due to poor dietary intake is rare, severe hypophosphate mia has been reported in children with kwash
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.4.1 Phosphate Deprivation

paragraphs.text: iorkor or marasmic kwashiorkor [203]. Up to 86% of children admitted for kwashiorkor in the Kenyatta National Hospital in Nairobi had hypophosphatemia. Following nutri tional intervention, serum phosphate levels decreased further during the first 2 days of treatment [203], suggesting a re-feeding syn drome. Serum phosphate levels of less than 1.0 mg/dL were described in a cohort of chil dren presenting with kwashiorkor in Malawi, where the severity of hypophosphatemia cor related with the fatality rate [204].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.4.1 Phosphate Deprivation

paragraphs.text: Hypophosphatemia may result from chronic ingestion of high doses of phosphate binder medications including calcium acetate or sevelamer [205]. Generally, mild or moderate doses of phosphate binders do not result in phosphate depletion. Use of medications such as aluminum or magnesium containing antac ids have also been reported to cause low serum phosphate levels, leading to osteomalacia and myopathy [206, 207]. The combination of hypophosphatemia with increased 1,25(OH)2D levels impaired skeletal mineral ization. Normal subjects who ingested a com bination of low phosphate diet and antacids for 3 months had serum phosphate levels as low as 1 mg/dL [206].
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.4.2 GI Malabsorption

paragraphs.text: Disorders where there is a decreased vita min D adsorptive capacity in the gut can also
paragraphs.heading: 20.3.4.2 GI Malabsorption

paragraphs.text: lead to lower serum phosphate levels. After small bowl resection and in Crohn’s disease, there is reduced surface area for vitamin D adsorption [208, 209]. Also, vitamin D defi ciency, leading to secondary hyperparathy roidism and mild to moderate hypophosphatemia, can result from steator rhea in cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis [210]. Patients who underwent bariatric sur gery have higher serum 1,25(OH)2D levels by 3–6 months post-procedure, where levels are significantly increased by 12 months. Circulating 1,25(OH)2D levels are higher in patients receiving Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch as compared with gastric banding [211].

paragraphs.heading: 20.4 Conclusion

paragraphs.text: Characterization of molecular basis of genetic and acquired disorders of phosphate homeo stasis has resulted in a greater understanding of the molecular regulation of phosphate bal ance. Phosphate is modulated by an interplay of different hormones regulating mineral ion homeostasis, where the manifestations of dis rupting the actions of these hormones have allowed for better insight into the molecular and skeletal processes which these hormones regulate. While significant advances have been made in deciphering the genetic and molecu lar basis for disorders of phosphate homeo stasis, major gaps still exist in the availability of appropriate treatments of the complica tions of these disorders.

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_20 ## PDF page 507 | printed page 500 ### 20.1 Introduction Extracellular phosphate is a critical compo nent of the skeleton that plays an important role in modulating skeletal processes like growth plate maturation and skeletal mineral ization. Phosphate homeostasis is regulated by dietary intake and the mineral ionregulating hormones parathyroid hormone (PTH) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF23). Furthermore, disorders disrupting phosphate homeostasis have resulted in a greater under standing of the molecular regulation of phos phate balance as well as the hormones that modulate these processes. ### 20.2 Phosphate Homeostasis Extracellular phosphate is a critical compo nent of the skeleton that, in combination with calcium, is essential for mineralization of newly formed osteoid. Growing children have positive phosphate balance to support skeletal growth, while healthy adults have a zero phos phate balance. Phosphate deficiency leads to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Phosphate accounts for about 0.6% of the body weight at birth and about 1% of body weight in the adult [1]. Eighty-five percent of phosphate is in the skeleton and in teeth, while 15% of phosphate is located in soft tissue and extracellular fluid [2]. In plasma, phosphate exists in either inor ganic or organic forms; the latter primarily as phospholipids and phosphate esters [3]. The total plasma concentration of phosphate in an adult is about 14 mg/dL, of which 4 mg/dL is inorganic phosphate (Pi). Ten to fifteen per cent of inorganic phosphate (Pi) is protein bound and the remainder is filtered at the renal glomeruli and is usually complexed with sodium, calcium, or magnesium. About 70% of phosphate filtered by the glomeruli is reabsorbed in the proximal con voluted tubule, while 10% of phosphate is reabsorbed in the proximal straight tubule, and <10% in the distal segments of the neph ron. Thus, the proximal tubule of the kidney is where a majority of the phosphate reab ### 20 sorbed from the filtered load [4]. Renal reab sorption of phosphate progressively increases as more is filtered, until a maximum tubular reabsorption rate for phosphate (TmP) is reached, after which phosphate excretion increases in proportion with the filtered load. TmP can vary even within the same person due in part to differences in GFR, therefore TmP is normalized to GFR (TmP/GFR, max imum tubular reabsorption of phosphate per unit volume of GFR), when quantifying renal tubular phosphate reabsorption [2]. In renal tubular cells, filtered phosphate is reclaimed by sodium (Na+)-dependent phosphate (Pi) transporters at the apical brush border mem brane. Phosphate is then translocated across the cell and returned to the blood circulation at the basolateral membrane, a process that is mediated by the Na+/K+-dependent ATPase [5] and possibly the xenotropic and polytropic retroviral receptor 1 (XPR1) [6]. Type II Na/Pi co-transporters include three highly homologous isoforms, including Type IIa (NPT2a, SLC34A1), Type IIc (NPT2c, SLC24A3), and Type IIb (NPT2b, SLC34A2). NPT2a and NPT2c, expressed on the brush border membrane of renal proxi mal tubules, are the predominant regulators of phosphate reabsorption in renal tubules. In mice, protein levels of NPT2a are approxi mately tenfold higher than those of NPT2c [3]. In contrast, NPT2b is not expressed in the kidney, but it is instead expressed in several other tissues, including lung and particularly the small intestine [7–10]. The ubiquitously expressed type III Na/Pi co-transporters are retroviral cell surface receptors (gibbon ape leukemia virus (Glvr-1, PiT-1, SLC20A1) and murine amphotropic virus (Ram-1, Pit-2, SLC20A2) that are [11, 12] localized to all segments of the nephron at the basolateral membrane and mediate cellular phosphate balance. Sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter type IIb (NPT2b, SLC34A2) plays an important role in sodium-phosphatedependent phosphate resorption in the small intestine. Type III sodium-dependent phos phate co-transporters PiT1 and PiT2 contrib ute to phosphate resorption in the small ## PDF page 508 | printed page 501 intestine, but less so than NPT2b [13]. Mutations in PiT2 have been associated with development of brain calcifications in humans and mice. Thus, affected individuals develop familial basal ganglia calcifications (Fahr’s Disease) and mice lacking PiT2 have elevated phosphate levels in their cerebral spinal fluid [14, 15]. About 60–65% of dietary intake of phosphate is absorbed by the small intestine, where in response to an increasing dietary load [1]. If an adult is in zero phosphate bal ance, the intestinal absorption of phosphate is equal to the amount of phosphate excreted by the kidney. In growing children, the net amount of phosphate excreted is less than the amount absorbed by the small intestine, thus resulting in positive phosphate balance [16]. Because serum phosphate concentrations vary throughout the day depending on dietary phosphate intake and oral phosphate supple mentation, collection of a fasting blood sam ple is preferred for clinical analysis. ### 20.2.1 Regulation of Phosphate ### Homeostasis ### 20.2.1.1 Diet 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 20.1 ### 20.2.1.2 FGF23 FGF23, a “phosphatonin,” is a secreted FGF and critical regulator of phosphate homeosta sis. It is predominantly expressed in bone, spe cifically osteocytes and at lower levels in osteoblasts [24, 25]. In the presence of the cofactor Klotho, FGF23 binds to FGFR1 with high affinity [26]. FGFR1 is the predominant receptor for FGF23 action, with FGFR4 likely playing a minor role in the phosphaturic effect when activated by FGF23 [27, 28]. FGF23 decreases serum phosphate levels by reducing expression of NPT2a and NPT2c in the renal tubule cells and decreasing the pro duction of 1,25(OH)2D. As documented in mice, FGF23 regulates 1,25(OH)2D levels by down-regulating expression of Cyp27b1, which encodes 1α-hydroxylase, and it upregu lates Cyp24a1, which encodes an enzyme that catabolizes 1,25(OH)2D, thus decreasing cir culating levels of 1,25(OH)2D. Tmem174, a transmembrane protein localized in the renal proximal tubules, interacts with Npt2a, but not Npt2c to prevent hyperphosphatemia, thus contributing to the regulation of FGF23 levels [29, 30]. Genetic linkage studies identified the genetic cause of autosomal dominant hypo phosphatemic rickets (ADHR), which is caused by FGF23 mutations affecting either Arg176 or Arg179 that render the intact, biologically active hormone resistant to inac tivation by cleavage [31]. In the presence of these mutations, iron deficiency increases intact FGF23 levels [32, 33]. Furthermore, some small, usually benign tumors excrete abundant amounts of FGF23 thereby induc ing urinary phosphate-wasting and osteoma lacia (TIO) [24] that is most likely triggered by expression of a chimeric FGFR/fibronectin protein [34]. Affected patients present with low serum levels of phosphate and 1,25(OH)2D resulting in clinical symptoms that are similar to those observed in other hypophosphatemic disorders. 35 ## PDF page 509 | printed page 502 2 like proprotein convertase [36] ( Fig. 20.2). Homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in DMP1 [38], FAM20C [39], and ENPP1 [40], as well as het erozygous or hemizygous PHEX mutations [41] lead to elevated circulating levels of FGF23 in mice and humans, and thus hypo phosphatemia. FAM20C regulates the phos phorylation of Ser180 in FGF23 which blocks O-glycosylation at Thr178, and thus enhances FGF23 cleavage [37]. ### 20 Glycerol-3-phosphate (G-3-P), a down stream product of glycolysis, is converted in the kidney, but also in other tissues, into lyso phosphatidic acid (LPA), which stimulates FGF23 production. It is conceivable that 2 G-3-P serves as a sensor for phosphate levels in the kidney, where phosphate stimulates kidney-specific glycolysis, and thus G-3-P and subsequently production [42]. ### 20.2.1.3 PTH Parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulates serum phosphate levels by increasing internalization and subsequent lysosomal degradation of NPT2a, thus promoting urinary phosphate excretion [43, 44]. On the basolateral mem brane of the proximal renal tubules, PTH binds to PTH/PTHrP receptors (PTHR1), which activates at least two second messenger systems, namely cAMP leading to the activa tion of protein kinase A (PKA) and intracel ![Source image](../../figures/ch020_p0509_01.jpg) Unmatched source image; PDF page 509. Both pathways then activate ERK/MAPK signaling to induce internalization of NPT2a [45, 46]. Furthermore, the PTHR1 can interact with NHERF2 at the renal apical brush border membrane, thereby stabilizing NPT2a protein on the cell surface and preventing desensitiza tion of the PTH signal [47]. Humans with het erozygous NHERF1 mutations may present with hypophosphatemia and renal phosphatewasting [48, 49]. ### 20.2.1.4 Vitamin D Dietary phosphate and serum phosphate lev els are important regulators of 1,25(OH)2D. Dietary restriction in rats or mice leads to hypophosphatemia, which enhances vitamin D 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) mRNA expression and protein levels in the renal proximal tubule by six- to eightfold [50], thereby increasing the produc tion of 1,25(OH)2D [51]. Furthermore, dietary phosphate restriction in mice decreases renal 24-hydroxylase activity and expression, thus 37 resulting in decreased catabolism of 1,25(OH)2D [52, 53]. On the other hand, treat ment of vitamin D-deficient rats with 1,25(OH)2D enhances NPT2a mRNA expres sion and protein in the renal brush border membrane [54]. Consistent with the findings in animal studies, dietary phosphate restric tion in humans increases serum 1,25(OH)2D levels, while phosphate supplementation has the opposite effect [55]. ### 20.2.2 Clinical Symptoms ### of Hypophosphatemia and Hyperphosphatemia Chronic hypophosphatemia is usually asymp tomatic, though affected individuals can com plain of myalgias. In mice, deletion of both PiT1 and PiT2 in skeletal muscle resulted in hypophosphatemia and muscle atrophy, dem onstrating that these phosphate transporters are required for skeletal myofiber function and survival [56]. Rhabdomyolysis associated with low serum phosphate is most commonly a consequence of chronic alcoholism [58, 59]. A combination of factors, including inappropriate phospha turia, gastrointestinal loss, hyperventilation, or infusion of dextrose-containing fluids, can contribute to hypophosphatemia in alcohol ism [57]. of elevated phosphate levels can be secondary hyperparathyroidism or the suppression of production of 1,25(OH)2D. ### 20.3 Disorders of Phosphate Hematologic consequences of hypophos phatemia may include hemolysis or leukocyte dysfunction. Adequate phosphate levels are necessary to maintain ATP levels in red blood cells and leukocytes [60]. Consequently, a fall in ATP levels from hypophosphatemia has been associated with decreased red blood life span, cases of hemolytic anemia [61–63], and impaired leukocyte cell function [64, 65]. 20.1 Box 20.1 Disorders of Phosphate Homeostasis Hypophosphatemia can result in respira tory muscle weakness, including impaired contraction of the diaphragm, leading to impaired respiratory function [66, 67]. In hos pitalized patients who had low phosphate lev els, improvement in respiratory muscle function was observed with phosphate reple tion. Severe, acute, or chronic hypophospha temia can compromise myocardial function [68, 69]. However, a study of pediatric patients with chronic hypophosphatemia from X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) demon strated no alteration in left ventricular func tion [70]. Central and peripheral nervous system dysfunction has been reported in patients with acute severe hypophosphatemia after developing re-feeding syndrome [71, 72]. Patients may manifest with irritability and muscle weakness and progress to confusion or coma [72, 73]. A high serum phosphate level is usually not associated with significant symptoms, but can lead to the formation of ectopic calcifica tions by precipitating in the soft tissues as calcium-phosphate deposits. Such calcifica tions are observed in chronic renal failure, hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathy roidism, or tumoral calcinosis, all of which are typically characterized by elevated serum phosphate levels. The hypophos phatemia can result in osteomalacia and rick ets, with bowing of the legs and short stature [74]. Therefore, phosphate supplementation and/or calcitriol treatment are used to treat the consequences of low serum phosphate lev els. Multiple disorders are complicated by Fanconi’s syndrome. For instance, majority of cases have an acquired form of Fanconi’s syn drome due to secondary causes that may include burn injuries, exposure to certain medications or toxic metals, or a variety of other conditions like multiple myeloma, or amyloidosis [74]. Furthermore, rare inherited disorders like cystinosis, Wilson’s disease, Lowe syndrome, type I glycogen storage dis ease, or galactosemia can lead to renal phos phate wasting. Medications like tenofovir, an anti-retroviral medication used for treatment of HIV/AIDS, is well-documented to be asso ciated with Fanconi’s syndrome-related hypo phosphatemia [75]. Patients infected with acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) who have severe disease requiring hospitalization may have a higher incidence of hypophosphatemia associated with acute kidney injury. It is hypothesized that SARS-CoV-2 infection involving the proximal renal tubules may lead to Fanconi’s syndrome [76]. Furthermore, Fanconi’s syndrome has also been described in families with fully pen etrant heterozygous missense autosomal dominant mutations in glycine amidinotrans ferase (GATM), an enzyme prominently expressed in the renal proximal tubules that regulates creatine synthesis. Affected patients develop Fanconi’s syndrome with hyperphos phaturia but no rickets or bone deformities as children, and they may progress to renal fibro sis and end-stage kidney failure as adults [77, 78]. ### 20.3.1.1 NPT2a Mutations The type II sodium phosphate co-transporter (NPT2a, SLC23A1) is expressed exclusively in the brush border membrane of renal proximal tubular cells. Deletion of Npt2a in mice results in enhanced renal phosphate-wasting, leading to hypophosphatemia, a decrease in serum FGF23 levels, and a compensatory increase in serum 1,25(OH)2D levels. The increase in 1,25(OH)2D increases intestinal calcium absorption and results in hypercalce mia, hypercalciuria, and suppressed PTH lev els [79, 80]. The age-dependent increase in serum 1,25(OH)2D levels correlated with the improvement of rickets in these mice, suggest ing that the enhanced 1,25(OH)2D action can compensate for hypophosphatemia in regulat ing growth plate maturation and growth [79]. An autosomal recessive form of renal Fanconi’s syndrome was described in 1988 in two siblings, who had marked hypophospha temia, and elevated 1,25(OH)2D levels, as well as rickets, growth retardation, and skeletal deformities [81]. Both siblings were later shown to have homozygous loss-of-function mutations in SLC34A1 (encodes NPT2a) and that their biochemical abnormalities greatly improved, although renal function remained abnormal [82]. Recently, numerous other homozygous or compound heterozygous NPT2a mutations were described in several infants, who presented with severe hypercalce mia and renal phosphate-wasting, and sup pressed serum PTH levels. Approximately half of the infants in this cohort had elevated serum 1,25(OH)2D levels associated with ## PDF page 513 | printed page 506 hypercalcemia. These metabolic abnormali ties resolved with phosphate supplementation [83], thus potentially preventing nephrocalci nosis. Mice lacking Npt2a fed high phosphate diets with or without high calcium were more likely to develop renal calcifications compared to wild-type mice fed a similar diet, suggesting that optimization of dietary content of phos phate and calcium are needed for proper treat ment of affected individuals [84]. Furthermore, two heterozygous mutations were identified in the SLC34A1 gene (A48P and V147M). The affected individuals pre sented with idiopathic hypophosphatemia, recurrent kidney stones, and osteomalacia [85]. Other heterozygous SLC34A1 mutations (91del7, A133V, H568Y) have been reported in a cohort of patients who have recurrent kidney stones but no hypercalciuria, hypo phosphatemia, or increased urinary phos phate excretion [86]. The likelihood of renal calcifica tions increased with the severity of hypophos phatemia and decreased tubular reabsorption of phosphate [92]. ### 20.3.2 Hypophosphatemic ### Syndromes of Excess FGF23 ### 20.3.2.1 X-Linked ### Hypophosphatemia (XLH) XLH is the most frequent inherited form of hypophosphatemia, with a reported incidence of 1:20,000 [93]. It is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern with complete penetrance, thought there is wide phenotypic variation, even within the same family. Establishing the diagnosis of XLH can be delayed until adult hood due to lack of awareness of phosphate levels or expression of a mild phenotype. When a more severe phenotype is present, children typically manifest rickets by age 1–2 years, causing growth retardation and bowed legs. On radiographs, the growth plates of long bones appear abnormal, with expan sion and fraying of the metaphyses [94]. There is discordant growth between the lower extremity long bones and the torso, with the growth retardation being more apparent in the long bones of the legs [95]. Children with XLH can manifest premature cranial synosto sis and often develop dental abscesses and caries due to defective dentoalveolar mineral ization [96, 97]. Adults may manifest with pseudofractures, osteoarthritis, osteophytes, or enthesopathy, which is the abnormal min eralization of the bone-tendon attachment sites, such as the Achilles or patellar entheses [98, 99]. Hypophosphatemia is often associ ated with myalgias, though many XLH patients are often asymptomatic from the hypophosphatemia [2]. As adults, XLH patients also report tinnitus and conductive hearing loss. Similarly, mice with XLH have conductive hearing loss, which is associated with hypomineralization of the auditory ossi cles [100]. 2 25 101 102 20.1 Hyp mice are a murine equivalent of human XLH. These mice carry a deletion in the 3′ region of the Phex gene [103]. The Hyp mouse mimics the XLH phenotype seen in humans, including biochemical abnormali ties, growth retardation, rickets/osteomalacia, and enthesopathy. ### Pathophysiology XLH is caused by inactivating mutations in the PHEX gene, which is located on chromo some Xp22.1 [104]. Over 800 mutations have been reported in PHEX [105], including mis sense, frameshift, nonsense, duplication, and insertion mutations [106, 107]. PHEX muta tions are catalogued on the website www. db.mcgill.ca. PHEX is predominantly expressed in bone, specifically in osteocytes and osteoblasts. It is also expressed in other tissues such as lung, brain, and teeth, but at lower levels [41, 108]. Although it is known that serum FGF23 levels are elevated in patients with PHEX mutations, the underly ing regulatory mechanisms contributing these FGF23 elevation are not known; PHEX does not directly contribute to cleaving and thus inactivating FGF23 [109, 110]. Although studies demonstrated that PHEX binds to ## PDF page 515 | printed page 508 and cleaves the triphosphorylated acidic, ser ine-, and aspartic acid-rich motif (ASARM) in proteins like MEPE to block their inhibi tion of mineralization [111], the physiological target(s) of the PHEX endopeptidase cur rently remains to be defined. Analysis of genetically modified mice have supported the pathogenic roles of PHEX and FGF23 in causing hypophosphatemia and rickets in XLH. Conditional ablation of PHEX in osteoblasts (using the osteocalcin promoter) leads to elevated serum FGF23 lev els, low serum phosphate levels, and decreased renal Npt2a expression, resulting in poor skel etal mineralization [41].
